newsitem.title: USA: Economists, consumers have modest expectations.
newsitem.headline: Economists, consumers have modest expectations.

text.p: Consumers' confidence in the economy is modest but steady at the start of the holiday shopping season, the Conference Board said in a report released Tuesday.
The private business research group said consumer confidence held steady in November after slipping in October and predicted healthy holiday sales in the coming weeks.

The board's Consumer Confidence Index now stands at 107.3, the same as October's upwardly revised figure. While the overall index did not change, the group said, there were shifts in its various components.
"Consumers are more positive about current business conditions than at any time this decade," said Lynn Franco, Associate Director of The Conference Board's Consumer Research Centre.
"This strong level of confidence coupled with low unemployment, modest inflationary pressures and continuing wage growth should translate into healthy holiday sales in coming weeks," Franco said.

In a separate report, the Philadelphia Federal Reserve Bank said economists projected the economy would grow in the final three months of the year at a 2.1 percent annual rate, which indicates that inflation is well under control.
The 37 experts in the Philadelphia Fed's "Survey of Professional Forecasters" said real gross domestic product growth would be 2.3 percent in 1996.

The two reports cheered bond investors, whose fears of inflation receded further. They pushed the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond up 22/32 of a point, or $6.88 for each $1,000 of face value, which lowered the yield to 6.38 percent from Monday's 6.43 percent. But it later edged back up to 6.40 percent.
The Conference Board said the expectations component of its November consumer confidence survey fell to 91.4 from a revised 95.7 in October.
Consumer confidence about current business conditions climbed during the last month.

Only 13 percent of all American consumers said present business conditions are "bad," down from nearly 16 percent in October. Nearly 29 percent described conditions as "good," up from 27 percent in October.
But consumers were less optimistic about the next six months than they were in October. Only 14 percent expect better business conditions ahead, down from 16 percent in October.

The group said the Rocky Mountain region continued to be the most confident in the nation. While the Middle Atlantic region still lags the average, it continues to emit signals of a rebounding economy.
The New England economy has posted the largest gains in confidence over the last 12 months.
The Consumer Confidence Survey is a poll of 5,000 U.S. households conducted monthly for The Conference Board by NFO Research Inc. of Greenwich, Conn.
